Sound is made by blowing or drawing breath through the mouthpiece so that the reeds vibrate; rapidly alternating blowing and drawing keeps the tone continuous. A beginner should first master closing and opening the holes or keys: on the traditional sheng the fingers cover holes in the pipes, on the keyed sheng keys or levers control them. It is also used in small ensembles such as the northern chuida wind-and-percussion bands and Jiangnan sizhu, and in the modern large Chinese orchestra it takes both melodic and accompanying roles. The traditional sheng is mostly a solo instrument, while the keyed sheng, being fully chromatic, suits the orchestra better. Composers outside China, such as Unsuk Chin, Jukka Tiensuu, Lou Harrison, Tim Risher, Daníel Bjarnason, Guus Janssen and Christopher Adler, have also written for the sheng.

The sheng is a traditional Chinese aerophone, a free-reed polyphonic wind instrument consisting of a mouthpiece and a number of vertical pipes, Hornbostel–Sachs 412.132. The player sounds it by blowing or drawing breath and can switch quickly to keep the sound continuous; the traditional method often adds a fifth or an octave alongside the main melody. It has long been used to accompany the suona and the dizi in solo playing, appears in opera such as kunqu, in northern chuida bands and in Jiangnan sizhu, and in the modern large Chinese orchestra it takes melodic and accompanying roles.
笙為中國氣鳴樂器，甲骨卜辭已見「笙」「竽」之名，約公元前7世紀《詩經》始見「笙」: The sheng is a Chinese aerophone; the names sheng and yu already appear in oracle-bone inscriptions, and the character sheng is first seen in the Classic of Poetry around the seventh century BCE. Ancient instruments with gourd wind-chests were excavated from the tomb of Marquis Yi of Zeng and from the Mawangdui Han tomb. In the eighth century three yu and three sheng reached the Japanese court and survive in the Shōsōin in Nara. From the early twentieth century Zheng Jinwen increased the pipes to 32, and Weng Zhenfa, Hu Tianquan and others improved the range and volume; after the 1950s the keyed sheng was developed, forming soprano, alto, tenor and bass members.
笙的發聲體為自由簧，古代笙有竹或金屬簧片，風箱為葫蘆，管體為竹。近現代改良笙在竹: The sheng's sounding body is a free reed; ancient sheng had bamboo or metal reeds, a gourd wind-chest and bamboo pipes. Modern improved sheng add metal pipes to the bamboo pipes to increase volume, and enlarge the wind-chest and the bore. On the traditional sheng the fingers cover the holes, on the keyed sheng keys or levers open and close them, but the materials of the keys, levers and other parts are not stated.
笙的音色溫潤飽滿，具有獨特的蘆葦簧片音質，既不如簫那般飄然若思，亦不如竹笛般銳利: The sheng's timbre is warm and full, with the distinctive quality of a reed: it is neither as drifting and pensive as the xiao nor as sharp and bright as the bamboo dizi, but carries a soft amber sheen. Its range is wide, spanning two to three octaves; the low register is deep and bleak, the middle warm and mellow, the high clear without being harsh. The sheng's resonance pipes produce a natural resonance, and when several reeds sound at once they form rich layers of overtones, giving it a harmonic function close to that of a piano. Compared with Western instruments the sheng's timbre is more Eastern in character, gentle and reserved; compared with the guqin it is more expressive and more penetrating, and it is an important harmonic and melodic instrument in the Chinese orchestra.
